Ordination: biplots and triplots

Source: vignettes/articles/ordination.Rmd
ordination.Rmd

ord_fit() fits every common ordination to long community data and returns tidy scores; autoplot() draws publication-quality biplots and triplots in the style of CANOCO. The ordinations are computed by the vegan package, so the results are identical to vegan’s (this is checked in the test suite).

library(tidydiversity)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(2026)

The concept

A community table has one column per species, so with 189 butterfly species every sampling day is a point in 189 dimensions. Ordination squeezes that into two or three axes that keep as much of the differences between samples as possible: samples close together in the diagram have similar species composition, samples far apart differ.

There are two families:

Family Question Axes are
Unconstrained (PCA, CA, DCA, PCoA, NMDS) What are the main patterns in composition, whatever causes them? The strongest gradients in the species data
Constrained or canonical (RDA, CCA, db-RDA) How much of the composition do my variables explain, and is it more than chance? Combinations of the explanatory variables, chosen to explain the most composition

Use an unconstrained method to explore and a constrained one to test a hypothesis. Comparing the two tells you whether your variables capture the main pattern or only a small part of it.

Choosing a method

Question Method method =
Main gradients in composition, short gradients Principal components analysis "pca"
Main gradients, long gradients (species turn over) Correspondence analysis, detrended CA "ca", "dca"
Main gradients from any dissimilarity Principal coordinates analysis, NMDS "pcoa", "nmds"
How much composition do my variables explain? Redundancy analysis "rda"
The same, for long gradients Canonical correspondence analysis "cca"
The same, for any dissimilarity Distance-based RDA "dbrda"

A first DCA axis longer than about 4 standard deviation units suggests long gradients, where the unimodal methods (CA, CCA) fit better than the linear ones (PCA, RDA). PCA and RDA use the Hellinger transformation by default (Legendre and Gallagher 2001); change it with transform.

Reading the diagrams

Element Meaning
Points Sites (coloured by a site variable)
Red arrows from the origin Species, in linear methods (PCA, RDA, PCoA, db-RDA): the direction in which each species increases
Red crosses Species optima, in unimodal methods (CA, CCA, DCA) and NMDS
Dark arrows from the origin Quantitative environmental variables; in NMDS and PCA they are fitted afterwards (passive)
Dark triangles Centroids of factor levels, such as years
Ellipses, hulls, spiders Spread of each group of sites
Faint dotted grey lines Label leaders only: they join a label that was moved to avoid overlap to its point

Constrained ordination: butterflies at Wanang

wanang_butterflies holds butterfly counts on 36 days over three years. Does the community differ between years and change through the months? Site variables (here year and month) are taken from the data automatically, because they are constant within each day.

butterflies <- mutate(wanang_butterflies, year = factor(paste("Year", year)))
rda <- ord_fit(butterflies, method = "rda", formula = ~ year + month)
rda
#> RDA of 36 sites and 189 species
#> Transformation: hellinger
#> Variation explained: RDA1 13.1%, RDA2 6.4%, RDA3 4.1%
#> Constrained: 23.6% of the total

Permutation tests of the whole model and of each term:

ord_test(rda)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   term        df variance statistic p.value
#>   <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Model        3   0.0521      3.29   0.001
#> 2 Residual    32   0.169      NA     NA
ord_test(rda, by = "terms")
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   term        df variance statistic p.value
#>   <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 year         2   0.0336      3.18   0.001
#> 2 month        1   0.0185      3.51   0.001
#> 3 Residual    32   0.169      NA     NA

How to read it. The printout says the year and month together explain 23.6% of the variation in butterfly composition (the constrained fraction); the rest is variation among days that these variables do not account for. A constrained fraction of 10-30% is typical for community data: species respond to many things at once, and counts of rare species are noisy.

The permutation test shuffles the days many times and refits the model; the p-value is the proportion of shuffles that explain as much as the real data. Both terms are significant on their own: years differ in composition, and composition shifts steadily through the months (seasonality), independently of year. Use by = "terms" for sequential tests (each term after those before it) or by = "margin" for the unique effect of each term after all others.

A triplot shows the days (points), the species with the strongest responses (red arrows), the month gradient (blue arrow) and the year centroids (triangles). Ellipses cover one standard deviation of the days in each year.

autoplot(rda, colour = year, ellipse = "sd", species = 10)

Interpretation. Days of the same year cluster, and the year ellipses overlap only partly: the community changed between years. The month arrow points along the direction in which days late in the season lie; a species arrow pointing the same way is more abundant late in the season, one pointing the opposite way early in the season. The angle between two arrows approximates their correlation (small angle = positive, right angle = none, opposite = negative). Read species only from their arrow direction, not from their nearest site.

Unconstrained ordination with passive variables

NMDS summarises composition without reference to the variables; adding a formula fits them passively afterwards ([vegan::envfit()]), as supplementary variables in CANOCO.

nmds <- ord_fit(butterflies, method = "nmds", formula = ~ month + year)
tidy(nmds, "envfit")
#> # A tibble: 2 × 7
#>   term  type      r2 p.value axes  permutations exact
#>   <chr> <chr>  <dbl>   <dbl> <chr>        <dbl> <lgl>
#> 1 month vector 0.198   0.034 1, 2           999 FALSE
#> 2 year  factor 0.185   0.01  1, 2           999 FALSE

How to read it. r2 is the proportion of variation in the NMDS configuration explained by each variable, and p.value comes from a permutation test. Month and year each explain about a fifth of the pattern, and both are significant: the main pattern in composition, found without reference to these variables, still lines up with them. That is stronger evidence than a constrained analysis alone, which always finds some pattern along the variables it is given.

autoplot(nmds, colour = month, group = year, hull = TRUE, species = 8)

Frogs along Mt Wilhelm

Frog communities turn over almost completely along the elevational gradient, so a unimodal method suits them. CCA constrained by elevation:

cca <- ord_fit(png_frogs, method = "cca", formula = ~elevation)
ord_test(cca)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   term        df chi_square statistic p.value
#>   <chr>    <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Model        1      0.959      1.44   0.001
#> 2 Residual     6      4.00      NA     NA

Interpretation. Elevation alone explains about a fifth of frog composition (model chi-square 0.96 of a total of 4.96), a large share for a single variable, and the test is significant even with only eight sites. In the triplot the sites are ordered along the elevation arrow, and the species crosses mark each species’ optimum: lowland species at one end, montane species at the other, with almost no species shared between the ends. That is complete turnover, which is why a unimodal method (CCA) was chosen.

autoplot(cca, colour = elevation, site_labels = TRUE, species = 12)

Which geometry for which kind of variable

An ordination diagram follows the same rules as any map or chart: the geometry and the visual variable depend on the type of data (Bertin 1967; ter Braak and Smilauer 2012; Oksanen et al.):

What Data type Drawn as In autoplot()
Sites, species objects points (or labels) always
Groups of sites (habitat, season, elevation band) factor symbols and colours per class; centroids, ellipses, hulls, spiders colour, shape, group, ellipse, hull, spider
Explanatory variable, linear continuous arrow: direction of steepest increase, length proportional to the correlation (vegan::envfit()) formula in ord_fit()
Explanatory variable, non-linear continuous contour lines of a fitted surface (vegan::ordisurf()) surface
A quantity at each site continuous symbol size (attribute plot, CANOCO) size

A continuous variable is a gradient, so it is drawn with lines (an arrow or contours) or by symbol size, never by colouring the points on a continuous colour bar. The same variable can be either kind, depending on the question. Elevation, for example, is continuous when you ask how composition changes along the gradient, and categorical when the sites are a few elevation bands or when elevation simply identifies each site. autoplot() treats a numeric colour or shape as classes (one per value up to eight, otherwise up to six classes), so give it a factor when you mean categories, and use formula, surface or size when you mean a gradient.

frog_pca <- ord_fit(png_frogs,
  abundance = abundance, method = "pca",
  transform = "hellinger", formula = ~elevation
)
# Elevation as categories: one symbol and colour per site elevation
p1 <- autoplot(frog_pca, colour = elevation, species = 0, arrows = FALSE) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Elevation as categories")
# Elevation as a gradient: fitted arrow and contours of a trend surface
p2 <- autoplot(frog_pca, surface = elevation, species = 0) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Elevation as a gradient")
plot_panel(p1, p2)
#> Ignoring unknown labels:
#> • colour : "elevation"

Customising the plot

Every option is an argument, and the result is an ordinary ggplot:

  • axes = c(1, 3) plots other axes.
  • species sets how many species to show (the best represented); 0 hides them.
  • ellipse = "sd", "ci" (a level region for the points) or "se" (a level confidence region for the centroid); hull = TRUE; spider = TRUE.
  • site_labels = TRUE, arrows = FALSE.
  • colour, shape and group take site variables.
autoplot(rda, colour = year, shape = year, spider = TRUE, species = 0) +
  labs(title = "Butterfly communities at Wanang, by year") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

Tidy scores for your own plots 

tidy(rda, "sites")
#> # A tibble: 36 × 7
#>    site    axis1   axis2    axis3   day month year  
#>    <chr>   <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl> <int> <int> <fct> 
#>  1 day01 -0.554  -0.0192 -0.548       1     1 Year 1
#>  2 day02 -0.585  -0.0395 -0.437       2     1 Year 1
#>  3 day03 -0.591  -0.0809 -0.531       3     1 Year 1
#>  4 day04 -0.423   0.167  -0.0389      4     2 Year 1
#>  5 day05 -0.337   0.0890 -0.00424     5     2 Year 1
#>  6 day06 -0.397   0.166   0.119       6     2 Year 1
#>  7 day07 -0.0705  0.466  -0.0135      7     3 Year 1
#>  8 day08 -0.139   0.396  -0.0547      8     3 Year 1
#>  9 day09 -0.150   0.361  -0.0338      9     3 Year 1
#> 10 day10  0.0778  0.443  -0.191      10     4 Year 1
#> # ℹ 26 more rows
tidy(rda, "axes")
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   axis  name  eigenvalue explained
#>   <chr> <chr>      <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 axis1 RDA1     0.0290     0.131 
#> 2 axis2 RDA2     0.0141     0.0637
#> 3 axis3 RDA3     0.00903    0.0409
glance(rda)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 8
#>   method n_sites n_species transform distance scaling stress constrained
#>   <chr>    <int>     <int> <chr>     <lgl>    <chr>    <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 rda         36       189 hellinger NA       species     NA       0.236

How to report it

Butterfly composition was related to year and month by redundancy analysis (RDA) of Hellinger-transformed counts (Legendre and Gallagher 2001), with tidydiversity and vegan. Year and month together explained 23.6% of the variation (permutation test, 999 permutations, P = 0.001); both terms were significant (Table S1). An NMDS with passively fitted variables showed the same pattern (Figure 2).

Report the method and transformation, the explained fraction, the test and number of permutations, and give the table of terms as a supplement.

References

Bertin, J. (1967). Semiologie graphique. Gauthier-Villars, Paris. English translation (1983): Semiology of Graphics. University of Wisconsin Press.

Legendre, P. and Gallagher, E. D. (2001). Ecologically meaningful transformations for ordination of species data. Oecologia, 129, 271-280. https://doi.org/10.1007/s004420100716

ter Braak, C. J. F. and Smilauer, P. (2012). Canoco reference manual and user’s guide: software for ordination (version 5.0). Microcomputer Power, Ithaca, USA.

Oksanen, J. et al. vegan: Community Ecology Package. https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=vegan
